summary: Extends the MRT format for exporting BGP routing data so it can carry optional geographic coordinates. The coordinates can describe where a BGP collector is, and where each of its BGP peers is. This helps researchers relate routing data to physical places.

eli5.summary: Imagine a list of mail carriers with a dot on a map for each one. This adds the map dots to the files that record how internet routers talk, so you know where each router lives.

subtitle: An optional MRT record type that adds latitude and longitude for a BGP collector and its peers.

tldr.problem: Researchers who study BGP routing data want to relate routes to physical places, but the MRT export format has no way to say where a BGP collector or its peers are.
tldr.mechanism: A new TABLE_DUMP_V2 subtype, GEO_PEER_TABLE (7), lists the collector and each peer with WGS84 latitude and longitude stored as single precision floats, and allows Not A Number values when a location is private.
tldr.outcome: Researchers can compare where networks are with where they sit in the routing topology, while operators keep the choice of withholding coordinates.

facts.label: Default retention
facts.value: 100 years from the MRT object timestamp

today: RFC 6397 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is an optional extension to the MRT format of RFC 6396.

sections.title: Why Add Locations to Routing Data
sections.content:
Researchers and engineers often study routing protocol transactions and routing table snapshots in relation to geography. Usually the subject is BGP (RFC 4271), and the data is stored in the MRT format of RFC 6396.

Adding the longitude and latitude of a BGP collector and its BGP peers gives a terrestrial view of the routes a BGP speaker sees. The RFC says this may help researchers understand the gap between where networks are located and where they sit in the topology, and the link between geographic position and routing anomalies. It could also inform future network design and network security.

The memo describes an optional extension to MRT and defines one new Subtype that carries the coordinates.
sections.eli5: People who study the internet want to know where routers are on a real map, not just how they are connected. This adds that missing piece to the saved files.

sections.title: Collectors and Peers
sections.content:
A BGP speaker is a device that exchanges routing information using BGP. A BGP collector is a speaker, usually passive, that stores and archives BGP routing data from active BGP peers for analysis. A BGP peer can be internal or external.

The RFC also explains how a collector works. It is a hardware or software device that speaks BGP and stores the routing data it receives from the speakers it peers with. Typically it only listens to route updates and does not announce or propagate anything. This is not always so: operators sometimes turn on collection on active BGP speakers to get a view of the routing system as they see it at one moment. As a full BGP speaker, a collector can fit into any BGP topology, including iBGP and eBGP.
sections.eli5: A collector is like a quiet note-taker in a room full of routers who are chatting. It writes down what it hears and usually does not talk back.

sections.title: The GEO_PEER_TABLE Record
sections.content:
The extension adds subtype number 7, GEO_PEER_TABLE, to the TABLE_DUMP_V2 type. The first six subtypes are the ones defined in RFC 6396. The record gives the BGP ID of the collector, its latitude and longitude, and a list of indexed peers with their own latitudes and longitudes.

The Collector BGP ID and Peer Count work as in the PEER_INDEX_TABLE of RFC 6396. After them come the peer entries. Each peer entry holds the Peer Type and Peer BGP ID, as defined in RFC 6396, followed by a 32-bit Peer Latitude and a 32-bit Peer Longitude. The entries in the GEO_PEER_TABLE MUST match the order and number of those in the PEER_INDEX_TABLE.

All coordinates are in WGS84 datum decimal degrees, stored as a single precision float in 32 bits.
sections.eli5: It is a list with one line per router: its name tag, then two numbers that say how far north or south and east or west it is on the map. The lines must be in the same order as in the earlier list of peers.

sections.title: Private Locations and Privacy Rules
sections.content:
A latitude and longitude MAY be a Not A Number (NAN) value, as defined in IEEE 754, when the location of the collector or peer is considered private. A pair MUST NOT mix real coordinates with NAN, so both are real or both are NAN, for the collector and for each peer.

The RFC also covers the GEOPRIV architecture (RFC 6280), which requires privacy rules to travel with location information. MRT geo-location has no place for such rules, so each location entry gets default rules in the style of RFC 4119: retransmission-allowed is True, retention-expires is 100 years from the timestamp of the MRT object, and ruleset-reference and note-well are empty.

Location information from an object with more restrictive rules MUST NOT go into an MRT geo-location record unless non-technical measures, such as contractual agreements between peers, enforce and communicate the limits on its use.
sections.eli5: If someone does not want to share where their router is, they can write "not a number" instead of real map numbers. And if a location came with strict rules, it cannot be put in the file unless there is an agreement to follow them.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
The new fields are descriptive, and the author believes they do not add a network-based security risk. Operators of collectors and peers are advised to think about their own privacy and security before supplying coordinates, with special attention to physical security if the resulting data is made public.

Coordinates supplied by a peer can only be taken at face value, because a peer may supply purposefully misleading or inaccurate values. It is up to the collector whether to include the data or to use its own methods to trust or validate it. The RFC does not recommend that a collector use coordinates that a BGP peer did not supply.

IANA registered the new subtype value 7, GEO_PEER_TABLE, in the MRT namespace for the TABLE_DUMP_V2 type.
sections.eli5: Location numbers are just what the router says about itself, and it could fib. So the note-taker decides how much to believe them, and nobody should be forced to reveal where a building is.

fields.name: Collector BGP ID
fields.desc: As defined for PEER_INDEX_TABLE in RFC 6396.

fields.name: Collector Latitude
fields.desc: WGS84 decimal degrees, single precision float, or NAN if private.

fields.name: Collector Longitude
fields.desc: WGS84 decimal degrees, single precision float, or NAN if private.

fields.name: Peer Count
fields.desc: Number of peer entries that follow.
